Industry observers note that although individual variation in protein amino acid sequences can exist between individuals, we find, among the regions of the proteins covered in our ancient data, only a single position with sequence variation among the worldwide distributed modern humans included in our database search (Table 1). In general, among extant hominids, out of the 43 amino acid positions variable among and between great ape individuals included, and in cases in which we have coverage for at least one of the four hominins studied here, only five positions contain sequence heterogeneity between the included individuals where at least four or more individuals of a single genus share variation (one position in H. sapiens, three in the genus Pan and one in the genus Pongo; Table 1). Notably, the four teeth carrying the derived AMBN A253G substitution shared with the previously reported H. erectus specimens from Zhoukoudian, Sunjiadon and Hexian differ from those six specimens, as the Naxian and Baxian hominins do not carry the derived AMBN M273V substitution (Table 1, Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Thus, the observation of the AMBN Gly253 substitution combined with the observation at AMBN Met273 in four hominin teeth, of at least three individuals, if the two M1s from Naxian cave represent the same individual, from two late Middle Pleistocene sites suggests that the hominin population to which they collectively belonged has not previously been sampled using molecular methods, either genetic or proteomic.

In a recent development, to further explore the phylogenetic placement of the Naxian and Baxian specimens, we conducted a Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. Note that, owing to the sparseness of dental enamel proteomic data, such analyses in palaeoproteomics generally have to assume that there has been no recent gene flow between the individuals and populations included in the analysis. We find that the four Naxian and Baxian individuals with the AMBN A253G substitution cluster together in a clade outside the branch of previously reported Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The topology of the clade formed by Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans matches the expected configuration in the main analysis, albeit with low internal node support (Fig. 4). The topology of these three hominin populations changes once additional modern human and great ape individuals are added to the phylogenetic analysis (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The expected topology of this clade is challenging to obtain when using proteomic data from dental enamel proteins, as reported previously29,39,40, and it is evidenced by the low support value of this clade in our analyses (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6). Nevertheless, the values supporting the nodes for the remaining branches, including the one placing the Naxian and Baxian specimens as an outgroup to the other hominins, are high in all analyses (>0.995). The Naxian and Baxian individuals are placed in a clade together with six previously reported H. erectus specimens. Those six specimens are placed together with strong support and separate from the four Naxian and Baxian individuals carrying the AMBN A253G substitution (Fig. 4). This strengthens the notion that these four Naxian and Baxian cave specimens represent a H. erectus hominin population that has not been sampled molecularly before. Furthermore, the phylogenetic analysis suggests that, although based on sparse data, this hominin population might have diverged before the divergence of the common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans. These phylogenetic observations are in accordance with the morphological analysis of these specimens, strengthening the case that these specimens belong to a previously unsampled lineage of H. erectus.

By contrast, proteomic analysis of PA1796 from Baxian cave reveals that this specimen does not contain the derived AMBN A253G amino acid substitution (Extended Data Fig. 6b). It has no uniquely derived substitutions compared to the other four teeth, nor does it share uniquely derived amino acid substitutions with the Denisovan, Neanderthal or modern human individuals present in our reference panel (Table 1). Phylogenetic analysis of this specimen places it outside of the H. erectus clade, with varying topologies with low support in relation to its placement in relation to archaic hominins (Denisovans and Neanderthals) or the clade including Neanderthals, Denisovans and modern humans (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 6a). The protein sequences reconstructed for this tooth are therefore different from the other four specimens studied proteomically, mirroring the morphological analysis that also indicates this specimen represents a taxon other than H. erectus. Only a single Denisovan genomic reference is currently available, the D3 specimen from Denisova cave, Russia, implying that our understanding of protein sequence polymorphisms for Denisovans is by definition limited. Future morphological and genomic or proteomic research on hominin teeth from the region could provide additional frameworks to allow more precise taxonomic classification of PA1796 into a non-erectus group, representing either southern Asian representatives of Denisovans (H. longi) or potentially another population or species.

Sources indicate that eight of the late Middle Pleistocene Homo teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves exhibit metric and morphological features that lie within the range of East and Southeast Asian H. erectus and that differ from those of Denisovans (H. longi), Neanderthals (H. neanderthalensis), or Pleistocene and Holocene modern humans (H. sapiens). The palaeoproteomic evidence provides further confirmation that four of these teeth indeed fall outside of the known genetic and proteomic sequence variation of H. neanderthalensis, H. longi and H. sapiens, but are consistent with a H. erectus-derived substitution recently described for Chinese specimens dating to around 0.4 Ma (ref. 13). The recovered proteomic evidence is therefore compatible with the morphological data. Dated to between 324 and 184 ka (ref. 12), these H. erectus teeth substantially extend the known temporal range of H. erectus fossils on the Asian mainland, bringing the extent of the mainland H. erectus fossil record closer to the latest known Javanese H. erectus, dated to 117–108 ka (ref. 8). The recovery of a unique proteomic signature of mainland H. erectus from the Middle Pleistocene of East Asia furthermore suggests that specimens attributed to this species could harbour several hominin populations13, and make it possible to molecularly test whether other H. erectus fossils from the region that could potentially date to the late Middle Pleistocene, such as those from Changyang cave (Hubei province, China)11,22 and Chaoxian cave (Anhui Province, China)23, also represent specimens belonging to the same mainland H. erectus hominin population, or whether they have a proteomic signature more similar to earlier H. erectus13.

The discovery of the Naxian and Baxian H. erectus specimens in the late Middle Pleistocene of southern East Asia enriches the hominin occupation scenario in the region. A Denisovan mandible has been described from the Penghu channel off the coast of Taiwan, dating to either 190–130 or 70–10 ka (refs. 7,48). In Laos, based on morphological analysis, a Denisovan molar has been described from Tam Ngu Hao 2, dating to between 163 and 131 ka (ref. 6). Genetic evidence on the timing of Denisovan introgression into the genomes of living humans also suggests that Denisovans were present in East and/or Southeast Asia well into the Late Pleistocene1,49. Moreover, several craniodental remains, such as Harbin, Penghu 1 and Xiahe 1, were identified molecularly as H. longi (Denisovans)7,9,17,19, and several other late Middle Pleistocene specimens probably belong to this population as well (for example, Xujiayao and Hualongdong), including also some non-erectus fossils from southern Asia (for example, Maba, Narmada, TNH2-1)6,50. It therefore seems plausible that the H. erectus population represented by the fossils from Naxian and Baxian cave on the mainland existed in relatively close proximity to Denisovan hominins.

Even though the geometric morphometric analysis of the EDJ suggest that the PA1796 M2 retains plesiomorphic aspects (mostly due to the short EDJ height), the specimen also differs from the morphology of the comparative H. erectus sample (Supplementary Note 2). The lack of a comparative sample for Denisovans (H. longi) represents a substantial bias in our ability to morphologically identify them. The non-metric morphology of PA1796 differs markedly from that of Chinese H. erectus by the lack of wrinkling on the EDJ, the absence of accessory fossae, the relatively large talon and the lingually shifted hypocone25,26 (Supplementary Notes 1 and 2). Moreover, the palaeoproteomic analysis of PA1796 demonstrates a different signal compared to the other Baxian and Naxian specimens, as well as to the six H. erectus teeth from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong13 (Fig. 4), strongly suggesting the presence of a hominin population other than H. erectus in Baxian cave. However, among the protein sequences available to us now, the PA1796 specimen does not exhibit the known proteomic variation associated with Denisovans, although it should be acknowledged that only a single Denisovan reference genome is currently available. PA1796 could therefore either represent a still-unrecognized H. erectus group that would differ in molecular and morphological aspects from the currently known H. erectus specimens, a hypothesis that we consider unlikely (Supplementary Note 2) but cannot outright reject, or belong to a non-erectus group, possibly related to H. longi. Future morphological and proteomic research on hominin teeth from the region, as well as the availability of a growing number of Denisovan genomes and proteomes, could therefore provide additional frameworks to allow a more precise classification of the PA1796 specimen.

In a recent development, the H. erectus specimens from Baxian and Naxian caves extend the geographical and temporal extent of mainland Asian H. erectus well into the late Middle Pleistocene. Occupying rainforest environments12, these H. erectus populations probably co-existed in close spatial and temporal proximity to southern Asian Denisovans. Mainland Southeast Asia therefore appears as a key region to study the evolution, genetics and archaeologically visible behaviours of multiple sympatric hominin species.

Sources indicate that the Baxian and Naxian hominin specimens were scanned using X-ray microtomography using the 225 kV micro-computed tomography scanner at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP, Beijing, China) according to the following parameters: 140 kV voltage, 120 µA, 0.5 angular increment one step and 360° of rotation. The final volumes were reconstructed with isotropic voxel sizes of 15.7–32.0 µm. A semi-automatic threshold-based segmentation was carried out in Avizo v.7.1 (FEI Visualization Sciences Group) and a volumetric reconstruction was then generated for each specimen. A full morphological description of each tooth can be found in Supplementary Note 1.

Dental surface models were imported in Geomagic Design v. X 64 (3D Systems, Rock Hill) to separate the crown from the tooth roots. The crown and roots were digitally isolated at the cervix using the cervix-best-fit plane as a reference51. Five variables were then measured or calculated: (1) Ve, the volume of the enamel cap (mm3); (2) SEDJ, the surface area of the EDJ (mm2); (3) Vcdp, the volume of the crown dentine and pulp (mm3); (4) 3DAET, 3D average enamel thickness (Ve/SEDJ; mm)52; (5) 3DRED, the ratio of 3D average enamel thickness to 3D average dentine thickness (Ve1/3/Vcdp1/3 × 10)53.

It has been revealed that diffeomorphic surface matching was applied to analyse the EDJ shape of the least worn teeth from Baxian and Naxian caves (methodological details are provided in Supplementary Note 2). This landmark-free, mesh-based approach was previously demonstrated to efficiently distinguish the EDJ of various hominin species6,22,27. Owing to occlusal wear, the apex of the dentine horns of some of the specimens had to be reconstructed before the analysis (Supplementary Note 2 and Supplementary Figs. 18 and 21). We first confirmed that the EDJ of the Baxian and Naxian specimens differed from that of Pongo and belonged to Homo (which was also confirmed independently by palaeoproteomics). We then compared the Baxian and Naxian EDJs to those of H. erectus s.l., H. neanderthalensis, H. longi and H. sapiens. The H. erectus sample includes dental remains from African and Asia that are regarded by some as belonging to H. ergaster and H. erectus s.s. (Supplementary Table 3). We indicated the labels of the H. erectus specimens in Fig. 2 to show the distribution of the African and Asian material in the morphospace. Canonical variate analyses were conducted and the Baxian and Naxian specimens, as well as the Denisovan molar from Tam Ngu Hao 2 (ref. 6), were projected a posteriori into the canonical variate analysis morphospace. Typicality probabilities were computed for the Naxian and Baxian teeth to provide a quantitative estimation of their most likely taxonomic attribution.

Recent findings suggest that for Naxian cave, fauna and hominin specimens were sampled using a handheld drill with a diamond-tipped drill bit, resulting in between 10 mg and 97 mg of powder for the faunal samples and up to 6 mg of hominin dental enamel. For Baxian cave, dentine was obtained using a handheld drill (36.5 and 43.2 mg of powder), while the dental enamel was sampled using an acid etch. All sampling and extraction steps were conducted in ancient molecular laboratories regularly used for ancient DNA and/or ancient protein analysis, including standard procedures to prevent contamination from occurring in the sampling and extraction environments, including wearing full body suits, hairnets, multiple layers of nitrile gloves, footies and positive air pressure.

Dental enamel extracts for Naxian cave were generated using 5% HCl, following previously published protocols31,54. Likewise, dental enamel extracts from the acid etching of the Baxian cave specimens followed previously published protocols54. The dentine samples of fauna from Naxian cave were extracted using a variant on previously published EDTA-based protocols55. For Baxian cave, the hominin dentine extractions followed a HCl-based protocol commonly used for ZooMS analysis, but with modifications to separate protein fragments by size9,56. Full protein extraction protocols are provided in Supplementary Note 3.

Industry observers note that faunal extracts from Naxian cave were separated on the EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) system coupled to a Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Hominin dental enamel extracts from Naxian cave were analysed on the Vanquish Neo UPLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) system coupled to a Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Dentine extracts from Baxian cave were first analysed on the Bruker Autoflex MaX MALDI-ToF MS instrument. Subsequent to the detection of collagen peptides, both the dentine and the dental enamel extracts from Baxian cave were analysed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Easy n-LC 1200 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) over a 120 min gradient. Blank extractions were included in all cases to monitor the existence of exogenous contaminants during the procedure.

Raw data files were searched separately by tissue type and cave site, using PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant in parallel. Initial searches in PEAKS revealed the possibility of a unique substitution in AMBN, while PEAKS and pFind informed on the composition of post-translational modifications (PTMs) that should be taken into account. After initial searches, final searches using an updated protein sequence database and updated PTM information for dental enamel and the full human proteome for dentine were performed (further details are provided in Supplementary Note 3).

It has been revealed that protein deamidation was calculated according to a previous study for MaxQuant data57. Other PTM ratio analyses were conducted by peptide-spectrum match spectral counts or peptide counts, unless indicated differently (applying to MaxQuant, pFind and/or PEAKS). Unipept analysis was carried out using all peptide matches against endogenous, dental-enamel-specific proteins58. As described above, a project-specific database was used for data analysis that includes protein sequence variation beyond that available within UniProt. As a result, Unipept analysis will not be able to match all peptides to the same taxonomic level as the one present in the protein sequence database used. Sequence reconstruction was performed for pFind, PEAKS and MaxQuant data jointly, resulting in a single protein sequence reconstruction for each specimen. Specifically, sequences from different search engines were overlaid for each specimen to generate a single protein consensus sequence. Amino acid positions where PEAKS, pFind and MaxQuant disagreed with each other were not called, and reversed to ‘X’. Positions possibly phylogenetically informative were manually inspected, fragment ion series were checked and E values were assessed. Where necessary, positions potentially introducing invalid sequences were subsequently removed from the protein sequence reconstructions. The consensus sequences were subsequently aligned to a subset of the PaleoProPhyler database of hominid dental enamel sequences, which included four individuals from each of the genera Pongo, Gorilla and Pan, as well as three Neanderthals41,42,43, one Denisovan44 and three present-day H. sapiens from the sub-Saharan Yoruba population. We also added the dental enamel protein sequences for Homo antecessor29 and Penghu 1 (ref. 7) (a Denisovan individual) and carried out Bayesian phylogenetic analysis of the Naxian–Baxian individuals using a combination of different proteins for each tree. The combinations are indicated in each figure (Extended Data Figs. 4–6 and Supplementary Figs. 33–43). The available H. erectus protein sequences from a single specimen (D4163) from Dmanisi, Georgia, were not included in the phylogenetic analysis carried out here because the phylogenetic position of the specimen could not be resolved in the original study29.

These fossils and their CT data are freely available to access for any researchers. #49389. Arsenal suffer huge early injury blows for Man City, Real Madrid as Mikel Arteta gives Bukayo Saka, Martin Zubimendi updates

📖 Baca

Arsenal suffer huge early injury blows for Man City, Real Madrid as Mikel Arteta gives Bukayo Saka, Martin Zubimendi updates

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (474 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 10:00.
  • Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has revealed that Bukayo Saka will spend another four weeks on the sidelines with the quadriceps injury he sustained against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.
  • Saka's injury occurred in the first half of Arsenal's 2-2 draw with the Bundesliga champions on October 21, and Arteta immediately conceded at full time that the winger's problem looked severe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 10:00.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has revealed that Bukayo Saka will spend another four weeks on the sidelines with the quadriceps injury he sustained against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.

Saka's injury occurred in the first half of Arsenal's 2-2 draw with the Bundesliga champions on October 21, and Arteta immediately conceded at full time that the winger's problem looked severe.

Reports emerging soon after stated that Saka would miss between six and eight weeks, although Arsenal have been loath to put an exact timeframe on the Englishman's recovery just yet.

However, speaking to the media ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Newcastle United, Arteta admitted that Saka was only halfway into his recovery process and would spend the full eight weeks out.

According to recent reports, "We had another test. It looks like it’s going to be an eight week injury more or less. He’s four weeks in now," the Spaniard told reporters.

Saka missing another four weeks means that the 25-year-old is set to sit out another seven matches across all competitions, including a number of heavyweight fixtures.

Arsenal host Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League next Tuesday, before ending the month with a clash of the titans against Manchester City in the Premier League.

Saka is also expected to miss matches with Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid in early December, and he will most likely be unavailable for the visit of Bournemouth on December 13 too.

However, the attacker could be fit to make his comeback against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United on December 20, until when Noni Madueke and Max Dowman will provide cover.

Dowman will serve the third of his three-game domestic suspension against Newcastle this weekend, but Madueke has earned numerous plaudits in recent weeks, having scored against Slavia Prague in the Champions League before firing the effort that led to Martin Odegaard's winner against Hull City.

Saka will likely be one of two core members of Arsenal's title-winning team to miss matches against Tottenham and Real Madrid, as Arteta also delivered negative news on Martin Zubimendi.

The midfielder appeared to hurt his hamstring in Spain's 3-2 Nations League defeat to England during the international break, and he also faces around a month on the sidelines.

"He has a problem in his hamstring. The scan shows there is an injury there he will be out for a few weeks," Arteta added on Zubimendi.

However, the 27-year-old is yet to start a Premier League game this season and was always expected to lose out to Declan Rice and Bruno Guimaraes at St James' Park tomorrow.

Arsenal are five points clear at the top of the Premier League table heading into gameweek 11 and are searching for their fourth successive win over Newcastle in the top flight.

#49379. Switzerland 4-0 Scotland: Swiss stroll leaves serious question marks over Sebastien Pocognoli as Scots round off miserable campaign with defeat on captain Andrew Robertson's record-breaking night

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1380 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

Switzerland 4-0 Scotland: Swiss stroll leaves serious question marks over Sebastien Pocognoli as Scots round off miserable campaign with defeat on captain Andrew Robertson's record-breaking night

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:06 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:08 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • Despite re-establishing Scotland’s credentials as a credible football nation, by common consent, Steve Clarke’s time in charge of the side was up in the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:06 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 18:08 EST, 16 November 2026.

Despite re-establishing Scotland’s credentials as a credible football nation, by common consent, Steve Clarke’s time in charge of the side was up in the summer.

With qualification for a major tournament no longer satisfying the desires of the Tartan Army, a seven-year itch led to a parting of the ways.

Industry observers note that in order to take that elusive step into a knock-out round, the theory went that employing a bolder coach who’d get more out of the players was all that was required. So much for that.

While few would dispute that a change at the helm was required, it was legitimate to question the wisdom in the SFA making one which was quite so radical. Those concerns have only been amplified by what’s been witnessed so far under Sebastien Pocognoli.

The Belgian is young, smart and intense. He won a title in Belgium with Union Saint-Gilloise and will have taken much from his brief, ill-fated spell at Monaco. He wants to play the kind of football supporters long to see.

Sources indicate that but this Nations League campaign has been nothing short of dismal. Two wins from six matches, both of those coming against a poor North Macedonia side, and three nights to forget against the Swiss and Slovenia, is a lamentable record.

Andy Robertson endured a miserable night on the occasion of his record-breaking 103rd cap.

Notwithstanding the fact that there were always likely to be teething problems, it’s fallen miles short of modest expectations.

Talk of it taking up to 18 months to all come up roses is all very well. But to believe that’s going to be the case, you need to see more green shoots at this point.

Having finished third in the section, Scotland are bound for pot three when the draw for Euro 2028 is made in Belfast next month.

Unless there’s a radical improvement come the qualifiers in March, it’s hard to see how Pocognoli’s side will get there by any means other than the back door.

This was another tough watch for the travelling supporters, one which will only lead to growing concerns about where all this is heading.

For half of a half, Scotland actually looked like they were getting somewhere under their new manager.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli faces some serious questions over a miserable campaign.

In a recent development, from the minute Lewis Ferguson scored a horrible own goal, though, they became a rabble. Not nearly enough punch on the front foot. And far too easy to play through.

They shipped two goals inside five minutes early in the second half and looked like they’d have taken the final whistle there and then.

Individual mistakes from players are troubling Pocognoli in the same way they pockmarked the later days of Clarke’s reign.

Having witnessed Grant Hanley, Scott McKenna and Andy Robertson err in the World Cup, the Tartan Army had already seen Jack Hendry sent off against the Swiss at Hampden before Ferguson joined the growing list of sinners here.

Arriving midway through the first half, his unfathomable moment came when there wasn’t a red shirt in close proximity. It was a kick in the teeth for Pocognoli after a reasonable start.

While it would have been stretching matters to suggest that his team were vulnerable, Murat Yakin was without four of his big hitters in Manuel Akanji, Johan Manzambi, Dan Ndoye and Granit Xhaka.

In a recent development, there was a smattering of starters with five or six caps to their name. Two of the front three, Samuel Ballet and Winsley Boteli, were just 20.

Lewis Ferguson can't believe his misfortune after slicing the ball into his own net for the opener.

It was a night when Scottish football history was made with Robertson winning his 103rd cap to finally rise above his great friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Pocognoli stuck by the back-three – Ryan Porteous, Luke Graham and Kieran Tierney – who acquitted themselves well against North Macedonia.

Industry observers note that there was no great shock that the more defensive-minded Aaron Hickey replaced Ben Gannon-Doak on the right. Without a goal in 21 matches before a ball was kicked, Oli McBurnie’s selection ahead of Che Adams was intriguing.

The infuriating thing from Pocognoli’s perspective was that his side began with the right attitude.

Aside from an Isaac Schmidt shot which was fielded by Angus Gunn, they looked comfortable.

John McGinn’s pass into McBurnie saw the Hull forward flick the ball into space for Hickey to chase. Just when it looked like he might get a shot away, he was caught.

The positive early approach was typified by Porteous flying into a tackle 30 yards from the Swiss goal and winning the ball.

Winsley Boteli enjoys the moment after putting the stylish Swiss two goals ahead on the night.

Had it not been for Hickey hesitating to pick out Scott McTominay’s run, the Napoli man would have been in on goal.

It has been revealed that to put it mildly, the Swiss didn’t need an invitation to go down. The appropriately named Samuel Ballet was especially fond of the theatrics.

For a brief spell, Scotland had their opponents hemmed in. Pocognoli was miffed that two quick corners didn’t amount to anything.

According to recent reports, billy Gilmour probed and McTominay made key interceptions and sprayed passes. McGinn fired over.

Recent findings suggest that at the midway point in the first half, there was much to admire. Then disaster struck.

The Swiss did well to advance down the right. Zachary Athekame simply launched a cross into the box and hoped for the best.

Aaron Hickey endured a painful injury blow and could now face another spell on the sidelines.

With Ferguson running back towards goal and Porteous waiting to boot the ball to safety, there was no obvious danger.

It has been revealed that for reasons only he could explain, the Bologna man stretched out a leg and watched on in horror as the ball sailed past Gunn. All that hard work undone in one desperate moment.

Hickey passed up a chance to immediately level when he headed Robertson’s cross wide. It was to be the Brentford man’s last meaningful involvement before he felt his hamstring tighten. Nathan Patterson replaced him.

A gift of a goal gave the Swiss a boost. Boteli introduced himself at Alvyn Sanches’ cross. Gunn was untroubled.

In a recent development, patterson did well to head Robertson’s deep cross back into the danger zone. McGinn’s header was straight into the arms of Yvon Mvogo.

According to recent reports, for all Scotland were entitled to feel a little sore at being one down at the break, it could have been worse. The defence were completely static as Adrian Bajrami released himself at a header. It was a good thing, from Gunn’s point of view, that the defender missed the target.

Alvyn Sanches drills home Switzerland's third goal in what was an entirely one-sided contest.

According to recent reports, ferguson truly had a night to forget here. Within two minutes of the restart, he needlessly invited pressure when he debuted a ball straight out of play.

Within seconds, with Porteous advanced, the Swiss broke down the left. Ballet fed Remo Freuler who returned the favour. Ballet rolled the ball towards goal from 12 yards with Boteli claiming the final touch. The visitors’ hopes of a VAR reprieve for offside were dashed.

And with that, the roof caved in. Patterson was dispossessed and Boteli worked the ball into the feet of Sanches. You could only admire the finish, but Scotland were an absolute mess in the build-up. It was threatening to get ugly.

Recent findings suggest that with Tierney, Scotland’s best player on the night, lying on the deck, Ballet was only denied by Gunn. The Tartan Army looked at the clock and wished it was over.

With a minute remaining, a bad night got worse when Zeki Amdouni’s deflected shot beat Gunn.

It has been revealed that mercifully, this tortuous Nations League campaign can now be consigned to history. It’s been the most chastening experience for all concerned.

Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb.

“It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play,” McBurnie told BBC Scotland.

It has been revealed that “We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored. I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

It has been revealed that “Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

However, the goal that would have made the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager’s debut as an international boss more memorable ultimately failed to arrive.

In this extended international break, the Scots will host Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday and then travel to North Macedonia before taking on Slovenia in Glasgow, with the Tartan Army hoping to see further improvement – and goals.

September 29: Scotland vs Switzerland.

October 3: North Macedonia vs Scotland.

October 6: Scotland vs Slovenia.

November 13: Scotland vs North Macedonia.

November 16: Switzerland vs Scotland.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, the debutant said: “Thought we struggled to get into the game first half, but second half we completely dominated the game.

Sources indicate that “They’ve got a top goalie who made really good saves. So many positives to take and a clean sheet as well.

“We changed shape a wee bit at half-time to get more control and that did really well for us.

“It’s a substantial game again on Tuesday so it’s important to recover now and go again.

“I’ve played on the left-hand side for a couple of years now, so I’m comfortable doing that.

Sources indicate that “We’ve had a great week. A new manager, new way of playing and new faces in camp. It’s just the chances we need to take - the fact we’re creating the chances stands us in good stead.”.

The striker told BBC Scotland: “It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play.

“We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored.

“I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

Recent findings suggest that “Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

Industry observers note that pocognoli’s first game in charge of Scotland ends in a goalless draw. The visitors produced a dominant second-half display, but their final ball and end-product was severely lacking in crucial moments. Ure, Hickey, Gilmour, McBurnie and Bowie all came close to scoring, but no one could break the deadlock.

Recent findings suggest that scotland cannot find a way past the impenetrable Oblak. There will be just two minutes of added time for the visitors to possibly score a late winner.

It has been revealed that lovric clatters into Gilmour and is cautioned. Slovenia can’t get out. It’s wave after wave of Scottish pressure.

In a recent development, oblak comes out and fails to claim Robertson’s free-kick. The ball is recycled and the Tottenham full-back whips a second cross into the box and Slovenia fail to clear. Welsh is waiting for it, but lashes a first-time volley over the bar.

Karnicnik catches Robertson with a late lunging tackle and receives a yellow card, giving Scotland a chance to get the ball into the box.

The hosts make their fifth alteration of the afternoon, with Cerin withdrawn and Lovric on instead.

Recent findings suggest that how has Bowie missed?! Gilmour finds Bowie with an outstanding pass through the centre of Slovenia’s defence. The substitute takes a touch then scuffs a rushed finish wide. Bowie has to do better there!

Another change is here for Scotland, with Gannon-Doak on to replace Hickey.

From the resulting corner, Oblak is there again to thwart McBurnie’s point-blank header. The referee then blows his whistle to relieve the pressure on Slovenia. Somehow, the scoreline remains goalless.

The hosts make another double change as Sporar and Brekalo depart for Vipotnik and Balkovec.

Welsh spots Bowie’s run and threads a perfectly-weighted pass through to the forward. From an unfavourable angle, the substitute’s one-on-one attempt is blocked by Oblak.

In a recent development, another massive chance for Scotland! McGinn’s searching corner is met by Hickey, who flicks a header wide of the far post. Scotland’s second-half performance deserves a goal.

Pocognoli orders Scotland’s first alteration of the game, with Bowie replacing Ure up top.

Hickey finds himself very high up the pitch and tries to tee up Ure with a cushioned header, but there isn’t enough power on the pass.

Gilmour and Ure link up effectively on the counter, but the latter’s pull-back is intercepted by Drkusic.

Slovenia then make two changes as Zabukovnik and Zec replace Elsnik and Drkusic.

McGinn strides forward and tries to find Ure, but Slovenia rush back to scramble it clear. Scotland are really pushing for the opening goal.

Gilmour and McBurnie play a devastating one-two, allowing the midfielder to advance into the penalty area. He shoots and aims for the far corner, but his placed effort is collected impressively by Oblak, who makes another crucial intervention.

In a recent development, the second half has started as the first ended, with Scotland applying all of the pressure. Slovenia have Oblak to thank for the goalless scoreline.

McBurnie and Oblak both challenge for the ball, with the Scotsman bumping into the goalkeeper, giving Slovenia a goal kick. The decision is met by a chorus of boos from the away fans.

McBurnie latches onto a loose ball and skips away from Drkusic’s sliding challenge. One-on-one, the striker tries to round Oblak, but the Slovenian goalkeeper does sensationally to apprehend him. Upon reflection, it looks like McBurnie should have just shot and tried to put the ball between Oblak’s legs. He did the hard part, but lacked a clinical finish.

The Napoli midfielder tries to float a pass over to the onrushing Robertson, but he hits the switch of play straight out for a throw-in. In defence of Gilmour, the pitch really doesn’t look in the best condition, with various players struggling regarding their weight of pass.

It has been revealed that we are back under way for the second half. Both sides are unchanged at the break.

Recent findings suggest that pocognoli’s Scotland finished the half as the better side, but an opening goal has proved to be elusive. At times, they’ve looked suspect defensively and have lacked rhythm going forward. However, Pocognoli’s squad have only been together for a few days and are playing in a newly introduced system. Can they produce a more inspired second-half performance?

In a recent development, despite Scotland’s late push for an opening goal at the end of the first half, the two sides head in level at the break. Slovenia started on the front-foot, with Sporar and Drkusic both going close for the hosts, before Ure struck the post to be denied a dream debut goal.

HALF TIME: Slovenia 0-0 Scotland.No goals at the break in Ljubljana.#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/6VGFRprBiz.

Ure strikes the woodwork! The Sevilla striker is agonisingly close to a debut goal for his country. He cuts inside to work some space and fires a low effort at goal, but his shot hits the post.

Scotland's best chance of the game so far 😯 Sevilla striker and debutant Robbie Ure strikes the post just before half-time.However, it remains goalless at the break.📺 Watch Slovenia v Scotland on BBC One 🇸🇮 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 pic.twitter.com/fm1wH2fOej.

Much better from Scotland! McGinn turns his marker and clips a wonderful pass over to Ure, who has drifted out wide. The ball is then delivered into the box toward McGinn, whose header bounces off McBurnie. Hickey is arriving to pounce on the loose ball, but the wing-back’s effort is blocked by the Slovenian defence.

Robertson picks up the game’s first yellow card for an off-the-ball incident. The Scotland captain is clearly very unhappy with the decision as we await to see a replay. Nevertheless, the action resumes with a Slovenia free-kick.

Slovenia go close again as a corner is whipped in. Drkusic wins the header at the near post and it bounces off the outside of the near post. That is definitely another warning sign for Scotland.

Matko goes on the outside of Welsh, and from a tight angle, he shoots, but his fizzed effort saves the side netting of the near post. Some fans behind the goal cheer because they think it’s gone in, but their view has really deceived them.

It’s been a quiet afternoon for both goalkeepers so far, with neither yet to make a noteworthy save. On a couple of occasions, Slovenia have had encouraging opportunities to get the ball into the Scotland’s box, but the deliveries have been overhit and poorly executed.

Similarly to Scotland, Slovenia are also playing a tremendously high-line. Unlike Slovenia, Scotland have been unable to find the right pass in behind the home side’s defence. Gilmour then carelessly gives the ball away as Scotland’s latest spell of possession ends.

Sources indicate that since Slovenia wasted that 14th-minute chance, Scotland have grown into the contest and are beginning to look comfortable in possession. However, they’re still waiting to craft their first notable opening here.

The hosts miss a huge chance! Once again, Sturm gets in behind Scotland’s incredibly high line and then fires a low cross into the penalty area. Sporar then beats McKenna to the delivery, but taps his close-range effort wide of the far post from inside the six-yard box. That’s a massive let-off for Scotland...

Matko is unleashed by a drilled pass then pierces through a gap between Robertson and Welsh. The Slovenia winger drives into the penalty area and tries to find either Sturm or Sporar with a cross, but Hendry does magnificently to make a last-ditch clearance.

Recent findings suggest that slovenia have the ball in the net, but the offside flag is up. Sturm gets in behind Scotland’s defence and slides a low cross into Sporar’s path. The striker then sweeps a composed first-time effort into the top corner. It’s a brilliant finish, but Sturm was miles offside in the build-up.

Sources indicate that gunn comes out confidently to collect a looping cross, before the ball is rolled out forward in McBurnie’s direction. The Hull City striker and Ure are playing really close to each other, very much like an old-school front-two.

Sources indicate that slovenia forward Sturm is wiped out by Hendry’s wild early challenge. The Scotland defender is perhaps lucky to avoid a booking. Welsh then heads the resulting set-piece away and out for a corner.

The hosts get us underway in the Slovenian capital. Can Pocognoli begin his Scotland tenure with a Nations League victory?

Sources indicate that both teams are out on the pitch in Ljubljana. We are moments away from the start of the Pocognoli era.

Newly introduced Scotland manager Sebastien Pocognoli sings Flower of Scotland as he takes charge of the national side for the first time 🎶 🇸🇮 Slovenia v Scotland 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿 is live on BBC One now.#BBCFootball #NationsLeague pic.twitter.com/I2aeqYkNGB.

Subs: Kelly, Bain, Binks, Doig, Christie, Miller, McPake, Doak, Graham, Bowie, Patterson, Montgomery.

"Let's go!" 👏#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/HBvPJdFkFb.

Luis Binks of Brondby, as well as Colby Donovan and Josh McPake, who play for Celtic and Hearts respectively, are all amongst the substitutes. This hopeful trio are all in line for their Scotland debuts if they enter the action later this afternoon.

Slovenski navijači se že zbirajo 👊🇸🇮#SrceBije 🇸🇮 pic.twitter.com/dM9UArGgl3.

'We're not going to be perfect right away but we still demand results'Scotland's Lewis Ferguson as the team begins a new era under Sebastien Pocognoli 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿#BBCFootball pic.twitter.com/42WCJh66gc.

On paper, it looks like Sebastien Pocognoli has opted for a five-back formation, with Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh making his Scotland debut as one of the centre backs.

Captain Andy Robertson and Brentford’s Aaron Hickey will operate as the wing-backs, with Billy Gilmour, Lewis Ferguson and John McGinn forming a midfield three.

A new-look attack is spearheaded by the returning Oli McBurnie and 22-year-old Robbie Ure, who like Welsh, will also make his Scotland debut.

Angus Gunn remains his country’s first-choice goalkeeper.

Sebastien Pocognoli's first Scotland XI to take on Slovenia 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿Watch the game live on BBC One Scotland from 13:45 BST 📺#BBCFootball pic.twitter.com/OnfWR7Gp8C.

Industry observers note that debutants Robbie Ure and Stephen Welsh are each poised for their first international cap. Billy Gilmour returns to the starting XI after missing the World Cup through injury and Oli McBurnie will make his first appearance for Scotland since 2021.

Sébastien Pocognoli's first Scotland starting XI 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/JC6RGOq1QJ.

“The first game is always a special game so you have to bring the mental aspect in for the players and for the staff.

“A good result can help but the most vital thing is we see things that we work on through the week. I hope is we apply that well then we will get the result which will be the perfect mix.

“I hope we can bring a good game, and a good exciting principle on the pitch. I think we need the support from the supporters because there’s a lot of fresh players.

“We need to create a good energy but it’s up to us on the pitch to create this. So then we can be hand in hand with the supporters.”.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

In a recent development, scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his newly introduced role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Darren Plant | 20 Nov 2026 10:04.
  • Burnley play host to rivals Blackburn Rovers looking for the win that would ensure that they avoid being cut adrift in the relegation zone.
  • At a time when the Clarets sit in 22nd position in the Championship table, Rovers return after the international break in 13th place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 20 Nov 2026 10:04.

Burnley play host to rivals Blackburn Rovers looking for the win that would ensure that they avoid being cut adrift in the relegation zone.

At a time when the Clarets sit in 22nd position in the Championship table, Rovers return after the international break in 13th place.

When Burnley stormed into a 4-1 lead at Cardiff City earlier this month, Fabio Celestini would have been confident that he was recording his first win as head coach that would also kick-start the club's season.

Instead, a 29-minute capitulation that resulted in a 5-4 defeat in South Wales has left relegation feeling increasingly likely, even though the season is only just under a third of the way complete.

Burnley remain on 10 points from 15 matches, their only success coming at fellow strugglers Watford, and they are already five points adrift of safety.

Although an upturn in fortunes would see them quickly haul themselves back into contention to avoid the drop, conceding 31 goals - the worst defensive record in the Championship - will not fill supporters with confidence.

Five of Burnley's seven Championship games at Turf Moor this season have ended in draws, but they remain the only team in the division without a home victory.

As for Blackburn, they have an interim management team in place after Tony Mowbray stood down from his position earlier this week due to health concerns.

Rovers sit 11 points above their fierce rivals in the standings, the pre-season expectation having been that the points difference would be close to the exact opposite at this stage of the campaign.

Nevertheless, Blackburn have won five of their last nine fixtures in the second tier to keep them in the hunt for a playoff spot.

The 2-1 victory over West Ham United in their last outing made it five wins from eight matches at Ewood Park.

However, Rovers have prevailed in just one of their seven away fixtures, a 1-0 success at Bristol City on October 13.

Blackburn Rovers Championship form:.

Celestini will inevitably make changes to his Burnley XI, with Max Alleyne and Josh Cullen among those who could return in defence and midfield.

Goalkeeper Max Weiss may potentially be handed a recall between the sticks in place of Gregoire Coubert, while Zeki Amdouni could start on the left flank.

However, Connor Roberts starts a three-game ban, a consequence of an incident at the end of the Cardiff game that led to retrospective punishment.

Despite Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds taking the reins from Mowbray, the Blackburn XI will look similar from the victory over West Ham.

However, second-choice goalkeeper Aynsley Pears is expected to deputise for Balazs Toth, who suffered a finger injury while on international duty with Hungary.

If the likes of Mathias Jorgensen and Ryoya Morishita overcome injuries in time for this fixture, they will likely be named on the substitutes' bench at best.

Burnley possible starting lineup:.

Weiss; Walker, Ekdal, Alleyne, Pires; Hatate, Cullen; Ramazani, Edwards, Amdouni; Hountondji.

Blackburn Rovers possible starting lineup:.

Pears; Beyuku, Carter, McLoughlin, Pickering; Morsy, Montgomery; Fevrier, Cantwell, Afolayan; Gudjohnsen.

It has been revealed that with Burnley struggling for wins and Blackburn having to adapt with Mowbray in charge, this points to a game where both teams would be happy to avoid a defeat. Therefore, we anticipate a low-scoring draw being played out at Turf Moor.

By Matt Law | 20 Nov 2026 10:10, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 10:12.

Barcelona need to make late checks on Jules Kounde and Pau Cubarsi before their availability for Sunday's La Liga clash with Villarreal can be determined.

Kounde has been absent since the middle of October with an ankle injury, while Cubarsi suffered a hip problem when he represented Spain against England last weekend.

Both have returned to training, but no risks will be taken ahead of a busy period, so the duo could find themselves on the bench rather than in the starting side.

Dani Olmo (adductor) is also close to a return but could ultimately just miss out.

Eric Garcia and Andreas Christensen could both be in line for spots at the back, while Marc Bernal and Fermin Lopez should join Pedri in midfield.

Anthony Gordon is again expected to join Raphinha and Lamine Yamal in the front three, with head coach Hansi Flick unlikely to spring any major surprises for this match.

Barcelona remain without the services of Roony Bardghji (knee), Xavi Espart (ankle) and Rodri (hamstring).

Barcelona possible starting lineup:.

J Garcia; E Garcia, Christensen, Martin, Cancelo; Fermin, Bernal, Pedri; Yamal, Raphinha, Gordon.

Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the genus Hordeum comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses1,2. Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during Hordeum diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into Hordeum, with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes Hordeum as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering upcoming avenues for barley improvement.

Recent findings suggest that the genus Hordeum comprises approximately 33 species and is widely distributed across the temperate regions of Eurasia and the Americas1,2,3. Hordeum is classified into two subgenera based on cytogenetic evidence: one containing the H and Xu genomes and the other containing the I and Xa genomes4. The basic chromosome number is seven, and, although most species are diploid, tetraploid and hexaploid taxa have also been described. Cultivated barley (Hordeum vulgare) is the best known and most extensively studied species, as it represents one of the earliest domesticated cereal crops. Today, barley is the world’s fourth most vital grain, valued for its use in food, animal feed and brewing5. Cultivated barley and its wild progenitor (H. vulgare subsp. spontaneum) constitute a single inter-fertile gene pool, allowing for frequent gene flow between wild and cultivated forms6. This primary gene pool has long been exploited by breeders to introduce desirable traits6. Hordeum bulbosum has contributed valuable disease resistance genes through introgression7,8,9,10 due to its ability to hybridize directly with cultivated barley. The other Hordeum species are not domesticated but have important ecological and agricultural roles in ecosystem stability, environmental adaptation and forage use11,12,13,14,15. Together, Hordeum is both an agronomically important genus and a powerful model for studying crop evolution, environmental adaptation and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. Factors such as incomplete lineage sorting, recurrent hybridization and gene flow partly obscure species boundaries, leaving major evolutionary questions unresolved1,2,4,16,17. Recent barley pangenomes have substantially advanced our understanding of genomic variation within cultivated barley and its closest relatives10,18,19. However, these studies were largely confined to two species (H. vulgare and H. bulbosum) and therefore could not resolve genome-wide evolutionary processes operating across the genus, including the origin of large-scale structural variation, ancient hybridization, polyploid genome evolution and the diversification of regulatory loci. Extending comparative genomic analyses to encompass the entire genus is therefore essential to capture the full breadth of diversity within the Hordeum gene pool and to facilitate both evolutionary studies and the effective utilization of wild germplasm for barley improvement. Pangenomics now offers comprehensive resources to address such complexity. In crops such as tomato, potato, maize, grapevine, citrus and cotton, genus-level pangenomes have uncovered extensive structural variations, gene presence–absence and evolutionary dynamics20,21,22,23,24. Investigating structural variations helps to explain evolutionary processes and can inform crop breeding strategies25. However, the full extent of structural variation within Hordeum remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we generated chromosome-scale genome assemblies representing all recognized diploid Hordeum species together with representative polyploid lineages. This comparative genomic framework provides a view of structural and regulatory genome evolution across the genus, yielding new insights into genome evolution and establishing a foundation for the utilization of wild diversity in barley improvement.

To maximize phylogenetic representation across the genus, we selected 27 accessions representing 24 Hordeum species, encompassing all recognized diploid genome groups1 together with representative tetraploid and hexaploid lineages (Extended Data Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1–25). The dataset comprises 22 diploid accessions, 4 tetraploid accessions and 1 hexaploid accession. Twenty-four genome sequences were assembled using PacBio HiFi accurate long reads and Hi-C data (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Figs. 26–28), using the TRITEX pipeline26,27. The sequence assemblies of H. vulgare and H. bulbosum were sourced from our previous work10,28. The previously published chromosome-level assembly of Hordeum marinum H559 (ref. 29) was updated using the TRITEX pipeline, and previously published transcriptome data, Bionano optical maps and Hi-C data of Hordeum erectifolium NGB6816 were used30. The average contig N50 of the assemblies is 39.24 Mb. Assembly sizes range from 2.90 Gb to 4.48 Gb (mean, 3.92 Gb) in diploid species and from 7.49 Gb to 8.56 Gb (mean, 8.16 Gb) in tetraploid species, whereas the single hexaploid genome has an assembly size of 10.90 Gb. Chloroplast genome assemblies range from 136,335 bp to 137,079 bp (mean, 136,840 bp) (Supplementary Table 1). High assembly quality is supported by an average long terminal repeat (LTR) assembly index (LAI) of 14.79, a consensus quality value (QV) of 67.30 and k-mer completeness of 97.22% (Supplementary Table 4). For the heterozygous diploid species H. bulbosum, the two phased haplotypes were designated as Hap1 and Hap2. For polyploid species, independently assembled chromosome sets derived from different ancestral genomes were defined as subgenomes and denoted as Sub1, Sub2 and Sub3 according to their phylogenetic relationships with diploid progenitor lineages (Fig. 1a). To assess the gene content in the Hordeum pangenome, we annotated all genomes using transcriptome data (Methods and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). A gene consolidation method was applied to ensure high comparability of gene predictions, including those for Hordeum parodii (6x) and Hordeum gussoneanum (4x). The number of high-confidence gene models identified ranges from 35,573 for diploid Hordeum murinum to 94,943 for hexaploid H. parodii (Supplementary Table 7). We assessed the quality of the Hordeum gene annotations using BUSCO (v5.8.0) with the poales_odb12 dataset, comprising 6,282 near-universal single-copy orthologues from Poales. On average, 97.35% of BUSCO genes were identified as complete, 0.69% as fragmented and 1.84% as missing (Supplementary Table 7). Independent benchmarking with OMArk and PSAURON further confirmed the high completeness and overall quality of the gene annotations (Supplementary Table 7). Transposable element (TE) annotation using the panEDTA pipeline31 revealed that transposons constituted on average 86.12% of the genome, ranging from 83.27% to 90.35% (Supplementary Table 8).

Industry observers note that based on the annotated gene sets of all species, we constructed a gene-based Hordeum pangenome. Overall, 42.4% of genes were classified as core genes, 56.5% as shell genes and 1.1% as cloud genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). Gene ontology enrichment analysis highlighted that phosphorylation- and kinase-related functions were enriched among core genes, ATP and RNA binding were enriched among shell genes, and defence response and oxidative stress response were enriched among cloud genes (Supplementary Fig. 29). Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) genes are key components of the plant immune system and have essential roles in resistance to fungal and other pathogens32,33. A map of their diversity is critical for advancing our understanding of disease resistance mechanisms in crops. Analysis of NLR genes revealed that I genome species contain significantly more NLR genes than the other Hordeum genome groups (Welch’s t-test, P = 1.8 × 10−6) (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). To further characterize this diversity, we constructed an NLR pangenome across Hordeum haploid genome equivalents (haplomes), comprising 800 orthogroups, of which 13.75% were classified as core, 27.75% as shell and 58.50% as cloud gene families (Extended Data Fig. 2c). In addition, NLR gene clusters were significantly less abundant on chromosomes 4H and 5H than on the remaining chromosomes (Wilcoxon test, P < 2.2 × 10−16) (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Similarly, genome-wide analyses of pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins and mitochondrial transcription termination factors (mTERFs) revealed significant expansions of restorer-of-fertility-like (RFL) subgroups in the I and Xa genome groups relative to the H and Xu genome groups. Because RFL proteins are involved in fertility restoration in plants carrying cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS)34, these expansions suggest that the smaller RFL repertoires of the H and Xu genome groups are derived rather than ancestral (Supplementary Fig. 30a–e and Supplementary Table 9). Expansion of RFL-PPRs was most pronounced in the I genome group, whereas RFL-mTERFs were significantly expanded in both the I and Xa genome groups. Notably, RFL-mTERF genes clustered on the short arm of chromosome 6H exhibited extensive copy-number variation between Xa–I and H–Xu genome groups (t-test, P = 5.2 × 10−6) (Supplementary Fig. 30f). This region includes the Rfm3 locus, which partially restores fertility in plants carrying the msm1 cytoplasm used in hybrid barley breeding35 (Supplementary Fig. 30g).

According to recent reports, to assess the feasibility of graph-based pangenome analyses across highly diverged Hordeum genomes, we constructed a pangenome graph using Progressive Cactus and hal2vg, comprising 2.53 billion nodes and 3.46 billion edges (68.7 Gb). Approximately 68% of nodes represented single-base variants, illustrating the extensive sequence divergence captured by the graph. Although computationally intensive tasks such as indexing remained infeasible (Methods), we successfully performed global analyses of core, shell and cloud sequence content, graph saturation, sequence conservation and variant diversity (Supplementary Figs. 31–34). These results demonstrate both the potential of graph-based approaches for genus-wide comparative genomics and the need for more scalable methods for graph exploration and interpretation.

Previous studies have inferred the evolutionary relationships among Hordeum species from plastome and partial gene sequences1,17. However, the relationships among some species remained weakly supported. In this study, we reconstructed a maximum-likelihood tree using a genome-wide single-copy gene set. Unlike previous phylogenies1,17, our species tree resolved all major evolutionary relationships with maximum bootstrap support, particularly among the recently diverged I-genome species (Supplementary Fig. 35). To further evaluate the robustness of these relationships, we reconstructed an independent coalescent-based species tree using ASTRAL-Pro3 (Supplementary Fig. 36), which integrates individual maximum-likelihood gene trees, and a genome-wide phylogeny inferred by CASTER from whole-genome multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) (Supplementary Figs. 37 and 38). We also estimated the divergence times of these species using fourfold degenerate third-codon transversion (4DTV) sites, excluding genomic regions identified as putatively derived from ancient hybridization (Supplementary Table 13). We estimated the divergence time between H and Xu at 10.3 million years ago (Ma), whereas I and Xa diverged around 9 Ma. The crown-group age of Hordeum dates back approximately 12.27 Ma (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 10). The chromosomes of Triticeae species exhibit high collinearity at their distal chromosome regions36, which is also the case in Hordeum (Fig. 1b). However, when aligned, the proximal regions show substantial loss of collinearity and highly fragmented alignments. Whole-genome comparisons across Hordeum species revealed that chromosomal rearrangements accumulated progressively with evolutionary divergence, contributing to the loss of collinearity and increasingly fragmented alignments in proximal chromosomal regions (Fig.1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a, Supplementary Figs. 39–44 and Supplementary Table 11). Quantification of reverse-orientation alignments across all Hordeum haplomes further demonstrated that putative inversions accumulated significantly more rapidly in proximal than in distal chromosome regions during Hordeum evolution (Supplementary Fig. 45). Among the seven chromosomes, chromosome 4H exhibited the most extensive loss of proximal collinearity (Supplementary Table 12). Recently diverged species retained strong chromosome-scale collinearity despite the presence of numerous structural variants, whereas comparisons between the deeply diverged H–Xu and Xa–I genome groups (more than 9 Ma) revealed almost complete fragmentation of proximal collinearity (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 3a and Supplementary Figs. 39–44). To estimate the size of non-collinear regions, we applied normalized coverage to identify these regions in species that diverged more than 9 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d, Supplementary Figs. 46–50 and Methods). In total, we determined the genome-wide distribution of non-collinear regions across chromosomes in Hordeum, with a cumulative size of 855 Mb identified in the H. vulgare genome (Supplementary Table 12). Given the central role of TEs in genome evolution, we compared TE composition between proximal and distal chromosome regions. Proximal regions contained a significantly higher proportion of TEs than distal regions (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10), primarily due to an increased abundance of LTR/Gypsy retrotransposons (one-sided paired Wilcoxon test, P = 9.31 × 10−10) (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Fig. 51). Together with the accumulation of large chromosomal rearrangements, these observations motivated a ‘stretch and twist’ model describing two complementary processes underlying the progressive loss of collinearity. The stretch component represents alignment displacement caused by TE amplification, whereas the twist component represents large-scale chromosomal rearrangements driven by structural variation (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

It has been revealed that in contrast to the dynamic structural variations found in proximal regions, the distal regions displayed more conserved, shared structural variations. This highlights that the extensive loss of collinearity in proximal regions precludes reliable identification of structural variants across more distantly related Hordeum species. Notably, large structural variations in the distal regions were predominantly inversions. On chromosomes 3H and 7H, we identified two large inversions spanning nearly the entire chromosome and present in multiple species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In total, 1,407 inversions larger than 2 Mb were identified across Hordeum species (Extended Data Fig. 4d). The construction of a comprehensive inversion map revealed six inversions on chromosome 1H that were unexpectedly shared across divergent phylogenetic lineages (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 5). We hypothesized that these large-scale structural variations might have originated from introgression events involving extensive chromosomal segments. We constructed a phylogenetic tree using the single-copy gene set from these regions to test this hypothesis. The resulting tree, resolved with maximum bootstrap support, confirmed that these structural variations are shared between one clade of the I genome group and the H–Xu genome groups (Fig. 2b). Moreover, 10 extant diploid Hordeum species diversified within 1.68 million years following the inferred hybridization event, whereas no comparable radiation occurred in other phylogenetic lineages during the same period (Figs. 1a and 2b and Extended Data Fig. 5). Notably, the alternative phylogenetic topology extends across contiguous chromosomal regions of approximately 200 Mb rather than isolated loci, indicating the inheritance of chromosome-scale haplotypes that are more consistent with ancient introgression than with stochastic gene tree discordance or incomplete lineage sorting.

To identify additional signatures of ancient hybridization across the genus, we developed a genome-wide scanning approach based on local phylogenetic discordance among single-copy genes. The single-copy gene set was partitioned into sliding windows, and normalized Robinson–Foulds (nRF) distance was calculated between local phylogenetic trees and the genome-wide species tree (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Peaks in nRF values indicate genomic regions with phylogenetic histories that deviate from the species tree and therefore represent candidate introgression events. Here, we define hybridization footprints as large chromosomal segments shared among multiple descendant species that consistently exhibit an alternative phylogenetic relationship relative to the genome-wide species tree. Using an empirical threshold of 0.21 derived from the genome-wide nRF distribution to distinguish discordance peaks from background variation (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 52), we recovered the chromosome 1H hybridization signal, validating the genome-wide scanning approach. Additionally, we detected more than ten consecutive windows with strong phylogenetic discordance signals at multiple regions (Extended Data Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 52). To further explore the underlying causes of these inconsistencies, we reconstructed local phylogenetic trees using the single-copy gene sets from these regions (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f, Supplementary Figs. 53–58 and Supplementary Table 13). Regions in which local phylogenies consistently supported a specific alternative relationship across a large chromosomal segment were interpreted as evidence of ancient hybridization. By comparing the regions that exhibited phylogenetic discordance with the whole-genome tree, we identified two large-scale segmental exchanges occurring within Hordeum jubatum, with maximum bootstrap support (Extended Data Fig. 6e,f and Supplementary Table 13). Surprisingly, this large-scale segmental exchange explains the major duplication and deletion pattern previously identified on chromosome 5H relative to the H. vulgare reference genome (Supplementary Figs. 12, 56, 59 and 60). The exchanged regions in the two H. jubatum subgenomes are each more closely related to different ancestral genomes, indicating that the apparent duplication and deletion resulted from ancestral segmental exchange rather than independent copy-number changes. (Extended Data Fig. 6d). In the allotetraploid H. gussoneanum, extensive segmental exchanges were detected between the two subgenomes on chromosomes 2, 5 and 7 (Extended Data Fig. 6e, Supplementary Figs. 53, 55 and 57 and Supplementary Table 13). In the allohexaploid H. parodii, subgenome 1 carried a large chromosomal segment on chromosome 7 derived from Hordeum stenostachys, whereas subgenomes 2 and 3 exhibited an additional segmental exchange on chromosome 4 (Extended Data Fig. 6f, Supplementary Figs. 54, 55 and 58 and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these megabase-scale structural variants preserve signatures of ancient interspecific hybridization and large-scale chromosomal exchange that are not evident from genome-wide phylogenies alone, providing new insights into the complex evolutionary history of Hordeum.

According to recent reports, genetic variation is essential for species evolution. Beyond sexual reproduction, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) serves as an evolutionary shortcut for acquiring novel genes. Traditionally considered rare in vascular plants, genomic advances have revealed widespread occurrences of HGT, challenging prior assumptions37,38. Our previous research demonstrated extensive HGT in Hordeum. Notably, species within section stenostachys (I genome; 16 out of 22 diploid species) possess ribosomal DNA (rDNA) acquired from grasses in the subfamily Panicoideae (for example, Panicum, Paspalum and Setaria)39,40. The oldest transfers (from Panicum), estimated to have occurred between 5 and 1.7 Ma, resulted in large genomic insertions on chromosome 5H, some spanning over 400 kb and containing TEs and protein-coding genes41. Here, we identified Panicoideae-derived nuclear genes across 20 diploid Hordeum species, with H. vulgare serving as a negative control39,41. Our analysis revealed 611 foreign genes that corresponded to 126 orthogroups, predominantly matching Paspalum (63%) and Panicum (22%) (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 14 and 15). The extent of HGT varied, with Hordeum flexuosum carrying the highest number of foreign genes (68 genes corresponding to 43 orthogroups) (Extended Data Fig. 7a). These findings align with studies indicating that grasses frequently exchange genetic material42,43. HGT frequency correlates with Hordeum phylogeny, with Mediterranean and West Asian species exhibiting fewer transferred genes than their South American counterparts. This supports the hypothesis that HGT has a cumulative impact on eukaryotic evolution44. The presence of a single panicoid gene in H. bulbosum and H. murinum can be explained by the introgression of chromosomal segment 1H from I genome species, rather than by an early HGT event predating the diversification of Hordeum (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 6c). Chromosomal mapping indicates that horizontally transferred genes are distributed across all seven Hordeum chromosomes, with chromosome 5H carrying the largest number (Extended Data Fig. 7b). These genes are significantly enriched in the distal regions of chromosome arms. Although distal regions generally contain higher local gene densities, negative binomial regression analysis showed that gene density explains only a small fraction of the observed variation in HGT abundance (pseudo-R2 = 0.034; Supplementary Fig. 61), indicating that higher gene density alone cannot account for the distal enrichment of HGT genes. Although co-transfer of genes remains uncertain, previous research suggests that large fragments of foreign DNA may be transferred together41,43. A substantial fraction (82 out of 126) of Panicoideae-derived orthogroups lack native Hordeum homologues, indicating novel gene acquisition. Functional annotation suggests that these genes may have roles in key physiological processes such as auxin transport, light response and transcription regulation. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis detected at least one expressed HGT gene in 73 out of 126 orthogroups (Extended Data Fig. 7c and Supplementary Table 16). The potential adaptive significance of these genes warrants further investigation. Our genus-wide analysis establishes Hordeum as a model system for studying the evolutionary impact of HGT.

The genome assembly sizes of Hordeum species range from 2.90 Gb to 10.9 Gb and are highly correlated with previous flow-cytometric estimates45 (Fig. 3a). After accounting for the direct effects of polyploidization, the haplomes exhibit pseudomolecule sizes ranging from 2.85 Gb to 4.68 Gb. Apart from a 19 Mb duplication detected in the subgenome of H. jubatum, no large duplication events were identified (Supplementary Figs. 59–60). A strong correlation was observed between total TE content and haplome size (Fig. 3b), confirming that TE accumulation has significantly contributed to genome size variation in Hordeum. LTR retrotransposons were identified as the primary drivers of these changes, although DNA transposons also had a role (Fig. 3c). Correlation analyses of individual transposon superfamilies highlighted that multiple TE families contributed to genome size variation, although overall TE abundance remained the strongest predictor of haplome size (Supplementary Fig. 62a). We selected transposons annotated in the TREP database with an average content above 20 Mb and examined their variation across different Hordeum haplomes. These TE families clearly differentiated the major evolutionary lineages of Hordeum (Supplementary Fig. 62b). To investigate lineage-specific TE dynamics in greater detail, we focused on three LTR retrotransposon families (BARE1, Sabrina and BAGY2) and used TEpop46 to reconstruct their diversification histories. TE subfamilies correspond closely to the major Hordeum clades (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b), demonstrating lineage-specific amplification histories that contributed to genome size evolution.
